items.title: In Event of Moon Disaster
items.summary: A memo from speechwriter William Safire to chief of staff H. R. Haldeman with the speech President Nixon would have read if Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin were stranded on the Moon. It also told Nixon to telephone the "widows-to-be" and had a clergyman commend their souls to "the deepest of the deep".

facts.claim: The National Archives holds the memo, dated 18 July 1969, in H. R. Haldeman's files (Nixon White House staff files); it contains the statement prepared for Nixon in case the Apollo 11 astronauts could not return.
The memo says the President should telephone each of the widows-to-be and that, when NASA ends communications with the men, a clergyman should commend their souls to "the deepest of the deep".
Jim Mann found the memo in the Nixon files at the National Archives and first published it in the Los Angeles Times on 7 July 1999 ('The Story of a Tragedy That Was Not to Be').

items.title: "I'm Not That Interested in Space"
items.summary: Part 1 of the recorded Cabinet Room meeting in which President Kennedy pressed NASA Administrator James Webb to make the Moon landing NASA's top priority. In it Kennedy says he is "not that interested in space" and that the only justification for the cost is to beat the Soviet Union.
items.credit: White House recording, John F. Kennedy Presidential Library (via NASA History Office)

facts.claim: The meeting on human spaceflight with Webb was recorded, but the recording was not released until August 2001.

A JFK Library news release (posted 23 August 2001) said the Library had opened the 73-minute tape of the 21 November 1962 Cabinet Room meeting, in which Kennedy made the Moon landing his administration's priority.
Kennedy said: 'otherwise we shouldn't be spending this kind of money because I'm not that interested in space' (transcript of presidential recordings tape #63, 21 November 1962).

items.title: The Kidnaping of the Lunik
items.summary: A 1967 Studies in Intelligence article on how US intelligence officers examined a Soviet Lunik upper stage from a touring Soviet exhibition and found it was a real production vehicle, not a mock-up. On a second access they borrowed it overnight, copied its factory markings and returned it before the Soviets missed it.
items.credit: Sydney Wesley Finer, Central Intelligence Agency

facts.claim: The article by Sydney Wesley Finer appeared in Studies in Intelligence in winter 1967 and describes how the CIA borrowed, examined and returned a Soviet Lunik from an exhibition touring several countries.
The earlier copy (CIA 0000609203) is stamped 'CIA Historical Review Program, Release as Sanitized, 18 Sept 95'.
This copy (CIA document C06355349) is marked 'Approved for Release: 2019/10/07'.

items.title: Soviet N1 Moon Rocket from Orbit
items.summary: A KH-8 GAMBIT spy satellite photo of a launch complex at Tyuratam (Baikonur), Kazakhstan, showing the Soviet N1 Moon rocket on its pad on 19 September 1968. The NRO later said GAMBIT images confirmed the Soviets were building a vehicle to go to the Moon while they denied being in a Moon race.

facts.claim: The Soviet N-1 lunar rocket (the CIA's 'J-vehicle') was photographed by an American KH-8 GAMBIT satellite on 19 September 1968.

NRO Director Bruce Carlson showed this Tyuratam image on 26 January 2012 and said GAMBIT images confirmed the site where the Soviet Union was working on a vehicle to go to the Moon, while the USSR denied it was in a race to the Moon.
The GAMBIT and HEXAGON programs were declassified in September 2011, but no images from them were released then; by 30 January 2012 the NRO had recently released several GAMBIT and HEXAGON images.

items.title: Project Horizon
items.summary: Volume I of the US Army's 1959 study for a military outpost on the Moon, prepared by the Army Ballistic Missile Agency. It proposed a first manned landing in spring 1965 and an operational 12-man outpost by late 1966 at an estimated cost of six billion dollars.

facts.claim: Lt. Gen. Arthur Trudeau's 20 March 1959 letter called a manned lunar outpost the Army's 'most challenging and perhaps the most urgent' space objective, needed for surveillance of the earth and space and so the US could deny Soviet claims on the Moon.

Volume I, dated 9 June 1959, concluded the US could make the first manned landings in spring 1965 and have an operational outpost by late 1966, manned by 12 men, at an estimated total cost of six billion dollars.
The volume's opening letter is stamped 'Regraded Unclassified by authority of Form DA 1575 dtd 21 Sep 1961', and its title page 'Regraded Unclassified, Order Sec Army by TAG'.

items.title: The DORIAN Files Revealed
items.summary: The NRO's 2015 compendium on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory, built around Carl Berger's declassified history of the MOL program office and an index of the documents released with it. MOL was a 1960s Air Force space station whose secret DORIAN mission was for two-man crews to photograph Soviet military targets with a giant camera; it was cancelled in June 1969 without flying a crew.
items.credit: National Reconnaissance Office, Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance (ed. James D. Outzen)

facts.claim: The NRO released a trove of declassified MOL records on 22 October 2015.

The release included 825 documents and 282 images; MOL was a manned spy satellite whose two crewmen would use a giant telescope to photograph Soviet military targets, and it was cancelled on 10 June 1969.
MOL ran for five and a half years and spent $1.56 billion but never launched a manned vehicle (NRO abstract).

rejected.reason: Already used by the nuclear topic as nuclear-project-a119; not duplicated here.

rejected.title: CIA Office of National Estimates memo 'Soviet Intentions Concerning a Manned Lunar Landing' (25 April 1963)
rejected.reason: Downloaded and checked (NSArchive EBB 479 Document 5, 10 pages), but it is a dry hedged estimate. The KH-8 photo of the N1 on its pad tells the Soviet Moon program story better.

rejected.title: Project Horizon Volume II: Technical Considerations and Plans
rejected.reason: 298 pages and 51 MB of engineering detail. Volume I has the summary, the Trudeau letter and the conclusions.

rejected.title: Meet the Astronauts of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (NRO panel video, 2019, Commons WebM)
rejected.reason: 846 MB, over the 400 MB video limit. It is also a modern panel discussion, not a declassified record.

rejected.title: MOL astronaut group photos and KH-10 DORIAN illustration pages (Commons)
rejected.reason: Every copy found is low resolution (about 300 to 900 px wide). The astronaut photos have no official source.

rejected.title: NRO MOL/DORIAN illustration PDFs (archive.org nro-dorian-mol)
rejected.reason: Mostly line drawings of panels and configurations with redactions, so they are weak visually. The NRO compendium is the better MOL item.

rejected.title: HEXAGON: Sentinel of Liberty (NRO film, FOIA F-2017-00169)
rejected.reason: Only mirrored through the Black Vault, with no official source page. The CORONA film has a National Archives record and a documented release.

rejected.title: Discoverer/CORONA mid-air capsule recovery newsreels (NARA 111-DD series)
rejected.reason: The catalog has only shot-list PDFs for these records, with no digitized video.

rejected.title: USAF Manned Orbiting Laboratory A/B rolls (archive.org, Periscope Film)
rejected.reason: A silent raw-footage upload by a commercial stock-footage house, with no official source.

rejected.title: A Point in Time, FedFlix copy (archive.org gov.archives.arc.1678526)
rejected.reason: The original is a 2.4 GB MPEG-2 file and the MP4 derivative is only 320x240. The 640x480 Public.Resource.Org copy of the same NARA film was used.

rejected.title: The Kidnaping of the Lunik, 1995 sanitized copy (CIA 0000609203)
rejected.reason: Same text as the 2019 re-release but scanned with no text layer. The 2019 copy (C06355349) has OCR text for PageIndex. The 1995 date is kept as the first release.

rejected.title: KH-7 image of N1 Launch Pad 110 under construction (USGS, 1966)
rejected.reason: An official USGS image, but it shows construction only. The KH-8 image shows the N1 rocket itself.

rejected.title: First CORONA image, Mys Shmidta airfield (1960)
rejected.reason: The Commons copy is 499x640 with no source information. The CORONA film covers the program.

rejected.title: JFK Library audio excerpt and the September 1963 Kennedy-Webb tape
rejected.reason: jfklibrary.org blocks scripts. NASA's History Office hosts the November 1962 recording directly, in two parts (Part 1 used).
